variants.name: Sequelize model version counter
variants.implementation_notes: Sequelize documents built-in optimistic locking through a model instance version count: set version: true on the model (or in the global model configuration) and each instance save()/destroy() is checked against the stored version, with a conflict throwing an OptimisticLockError; the feature is disabled by default, so it must be switched on per model. The classic session/validator structure is replaced by the framework's instance methods - but only for instance writes, not for static bulk calls.
pitfalls: version: true guards instance save/destroy only - static Model.update()/destroy() execute a bulk statement and bypass the check.
Because the option is off by default, a model that forgets it looks identical at runtime while silently allowing lost updates.
Sequelize reports the conflict by throwing OptimisticLockError: catch it explicitly, re-read the row, and keep the retry bounded - retrying with the same stale instance fails every time.

variants.name: node-postgres guarded statement
variants.implementation_notes: With bare pg the pattern is one guarded statement: client.query returns a pg.Result whose rowCount comes from PostgreSQL's command tag and reflects the rows the command modified, so rowCount === 0 is the conflict signal. Keep it in one client transaction and always bump the version in the SET list, otherwise the row keeps its token and the next stale writer succeeds.
pitfalls: rowCount is null for commands with no row tag (e.g. LOCK) and counts rows modified, not rows returned - never compare it with rows.length.
Run the statement on the same client inside a transaction; a pooled query can land on another connection with different session state.
Without version = version + 1 the same row can be overwritten repeatedly: the token never moves, so no later writer is ever rejected.
